summary: Defines how the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) produces, reviews, and publishes its own documents as RFCs. The IAB occasionally issues statements and architectural guidance, and this memo sets out the process those documents follow on their way into the RFC Series.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of advisers sometimes writes official notes for everyone to read. This note is the checklist that says how those notes get written, checked by others, and finally printed.

questions: how does the iab publish rfcs
what is the iab call for comment
subtitle: How the Internet Architecture Board gets its own documents reviewed and published as RFCs.

tldr.problem: The IAB publishes statements, workshop reports and other documents as RFCs, and needed a written process for how they are produced, reviewed and approved.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB publishes a draft, the IAB chair issues an IETF-wide Call for Comment (normally no shorter than four weeks), the IAB weighs the comments, and then the document goes to the RFC Editor.
tldr.outcome: Most IAB documents become Informational RFCs. The document describes a process only and has no security implications.

facts.label: Call for Comment
facts.value: Normally no shorter than four weeks

today: RFC 4845 is an Informational RFC published in July 2007. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: When the IAB Publishes RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 4845 describes how the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) publishes documents in the RFC Series. It names three occasions: documents that come out of IAB consideration of an issue and are authored by the IAB through a nominated editor; reports on IAB activities, such as workshop reports; and documents that are not the outcome of an IETF Working Group but that the IAB decides would benefit the IETF community.

Most IAB documents are Informational RFCs. Generally, the IAB does not publish Standards-Track or Experimental RFCs. A Best Current Practice (BCP) from the IAB falls under the approval process of the IETF standards stream, as described in RFC 4844.
sections.plainLanguage: The advisers write notes for different reasons: to share their own views, to report on a meeting, or to share something useful from someone else. Most notes are just for information.

sections.title: Review and Approval
sections.content:
When a document records an IAB statement or position, the IAB refines it through its internal discussion and approves it for publication if, and only if, the IAB is in agreement on its substantive content.

For some documents the IAB does not take responsibility for technical correctness. For a workshop report where not all participants were IAB members, IAB approval only asserts that the report is a faithful report of the proceedings and that the matter is of interest to the community.

Documents for which the IAB takes responsibility for technical correctness, the most usual case, list the IAB as an author, with individuals as editors or text authors. Other documents, such as workshop reports, do not name the IAB as an author. The introductory text should make the IAB's role plain, and a note may be added if the IAB has significant issues with an item.
sections.plainLanguage: If the advisers all agree, the note speaks for them and has their name on it. If it is only a report of a meeting, they just promise it is an honest report.

sections.title: The Publication Steps
sections.content:
The process has seven steps. The IAB first decides a document is an IAB document, then publishes an IAB draft (draft-iab-*) and reviews comments on it. It may also ask individuals or groups for comments.

A document intended as a BCP is passed to the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) with a sponsoring Area Director. For Informational RFCs, the IAB chair issues an IETF-wide Call for Comment on the IETF Announce mailing list, and the comment period is normally no shorter than four weeks.

The IAB then decides whether the comments show the document is ready or whether another round of editing, and optionally a further call for input, is needed. When it is ready, the document is passed to the RFC Editor for publication as an IAB document Informational RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: First the advisers share a draft. Then they ask everyone to comment for at least about four weeks, fix what people point out, and finally hand it over to be printed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that it does not discuss matters with any particular security implications. It is a description of a publication process.
sections.plainLanguage: This note is only about paperwork, so it has nothing to say about keeping things safe.
